Newborn Care

Breastfeeding and newborn jaundice: keeping feeding and treatment together

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A yellow tinge in a newborn is common, but the timing, bilirubin level and baby’s condition determine what care is needed. Breastfeeding can usually continue. The aim is to make sure the baby receives enough milk while arranging the right tests and treatment, rather than treating feeding support and medical care as separate choices.

Why a newborn can look yellow

Jaundice is the yellow colour caused by a build-up of bilirubin, a substance formed when red blood cells are broken down. The liver normally processes bilirubin so it can leave the body through bile and the gut. In the first days of life, babies produce relatively large amounts and their liver is still becoming more efficient at handling it.

Jaundice is common: estimates often quoted are around 60% of babies born at term and 80% of premature babies in the first week. Most cases are temporary, but common does not mean that every case is safe to watch without advice. A clinician needs to consider when it began, the bilirubin measurement and how the baby is doing.

Timing helps, but does not give the diagnosis by itself

Ordinary newborn jaundice often becomes visible after the first 24 hours and is most noticeable over the next few days. It may last longer in babies born early. A baby who is feeding and gaining weight well can still need a bilirubin check; apparent wellbeing does not replace the measurement when jaundice is suspected.

Jaundice during the first 24 hours needs urgent medical assessment because it may have a more serious cause. Contact the maternity or newborn service promptly for new or worsening yellowing at any age. Do not wait for the colour to reach the legs, or assume that a particular birth weight makes jaundice harmless.

There are several reasons bilirubin can rise

Prematurity, bruising or bleeding around the birth, and having more red blood cells than usual can increase the bilirubin load. A sibling who needed jaundice treatment is useful family history. Maternal diabetes and the baby’s growth and birth history may also influence the team’s assessment.

Sometimes red blood cells break down too quickly. Possible causes include certain maternal–infant blood-group incompatibilities, G6PD enzyme deficiency and inherited red-cell membrane disorders. An ABO or Rh difference does not automatically mean harmful haemolysis has occurred; examination and tests determine whether it is relevant.

Other causes include infection, including some infections acquired before birth, liver or bile-duct disease, hypothyroidism and metabolic conditions such as galactosaemia. These are not all equally likely, but they explain why prolonged or unusual jaundice should not simply be labelled a feeding issue. Routine newborn screening results can be important to review.

Early low-intake jaundice is a feeding problem to assess

In the first week, a baby who receives too little milk may pass less stool and reabsorb more bilirubin from the gut. This is often called suboptimal-intake jaundice. It can happen when attachment or milk transfer is ineffective, feeds are too infrequent, or a sleepy baby struggles to feed. It does not mean breast milk is inherently harmful.

Ask someone skilled in infant feeding to observe a full feed and assess weight change, swallowing and nappy output. Simply counting minutes at the breast can miss poor transfer. A parent who needs help establishing feeding should receive practical support, not blame or reassurance without checking whether the baby is actually getting enough.

Breast-milk jaundice is a different pattern

Breast-milk jaundice usually appears or persists later, often into the second and subsequent weeks, in a baby who may otherwise feed and grow well. The mechanisms are not fully understood. Several influences on bilirubin processing and reabsorption have been proposed, so it should not be described as one proven enzyme problem in every baby.

The name is used after appropriate assessment, not as a reason to overlook liver disease, infection or inadequate intake. Yellowing can persist for several weeks, but the baby still needs the recommended review and tests. Most babies with this pattern can continue breastfeeding.

Watch the whole baby, not only the skin colour

Yellowing may be easier to see in the whites of the eyes or gums, especially when a skin-colour change is less obvious. Good light helps observation, but looking at the skin cannot tell you the bilirubin concentration. A skin meter or blood test may be needed; treatment decisions sometimes require a blood measurement even after a skin reading.

Seek urgent help if the baby is increasingly sleepy, difficult to wake, feeding poorly or producing fewer wet nappies than expected. A weak or unusual cry, marked floppiness, fever or seeming generally unwell also needs prompt assessment. Dark urine that stains the nappy or pale, chalky stools is a warning sign even if the baby otherwise seems comfortable.

A baby who is unresponsive, has a seizure, has trouble breathing, becomes very stiff or arches backwards, or develops abnormal eye movements needs emergency care. Severe bilirubin-related illness can injure the brain and hearing, but prompt recognition and appropriate treatment greatly change the situation. Do not wait for a scheduled blood test if the baby deteriorates.

A bilirubin number needs age and risk information

There is no single bilirubin value that decides treatment for all newborns. Clinicians use the baby’s age in hours, gestational age, current level and rate of rise, together with risk factors such as haemolysis or significant illness. The same result can lead to different decisions in a younger or more vulnerable baby.

This is why a fixed rule such as “home treatment below this number” or “brain injury above that number” can be misleading. Laboratories also report different units, commonly mg/dL or micromoles per litre. Ask the team to explain the result using the correct chart and units rather than comparing it with a number found online.

The American Academy of Pediatrics guideline applies to babies born at 35 weeks or later; babies born earlier need specialist protocols. Other countries use their own guidance. The care team should make clear which threshold chart and follow-up plan apply to your baby.

Keep feeding support alongside jaundice treatment

Many breastfed newborns feed eight to twelve times in 24 hours, with an individual plan if sleepiness or poor transfer interferes. A clinician may advise waking for feeds while the problem is being addressed. Track feeds and nappies as instructed, but seek help rather than relying on a record when the baby looks unwell.

If extra milk is needed, the team may recommend expressed milk, appropriately sourced donor milk or infant formula, depending on urgency, availability and the baby’s condition. Supplementation is a treatment decision, not a judgment about a parent’s effort. Ask how to protect milk production if the baby is not feeding effectively at the breast.

Do not use water, sugar water or herbal remedies to clear jaundice. These do not provide an appropriate substitute for milk or bilirubin treatment. Feeding support and medical treatment can happen together; a baby should not be left waiting for milk supply to improve if bilirubin has reached a treatment threshold.

Phototherapy uses prescribed light and monitoring

Phototherapy exposes the baby to a controlled light source that changes bilirubin into forms the body can eliminate more easily. It is usually delivered with special blue-light equipment, including certain LED systems or fibre-optic devices. It is not the same as ultraviolet tanning light or placing a baby in direct sunlight.

The team decides how much skin needs exposure and gives instructions about positioning, feeding breaks, temperature checks and any eye protection required for that particular device. Follow those directions; a blanket or light placed at an improvised distance may not deliver the intended treatment.

Repeat bilirubin measurements show whether treatment is working and when it can stop. Some babies need a further measurement after stopping because the level can rise again. If bilirubin approaches a dangerous threshold or there are neurological signs, urgent hospital escalation is needed. An exchange transfusion is reserved for specific severe circumstances, not triggered by one universal number for every baby.

Home phototherapy is suitable only for selected babies

Home treatment requires a medical assessment, suitable equipment, dependable follow-up and a family able to use the system safely. It is not simply a lamp rented because a baby looks yellow. Prematurity, illness, inadequate feeding, rapidly rising bilirubin or other risk factors can make hospital treatment more appropriate.

One AAP pathway for a discharged baby limits home treatment to those born at least 38 weeks, at least 48 hours old, clinically well and feeding adequately, without bilirubin neurotoxicity risk factors or previous phototherapy. It also requires a level only slightly above the appropriate treatment threshold, prompt access to an LED device and daily blood bilirubin testing. Local services may use different eligibility rules.

Before going home, know who will review each result, where the next sample will be taken, how to use and troubleshoot the device, and what symptoms or results require hospital care. If the light stops working or you cannot attend monitoring, contact the service immediately. Do not compensate by changing the setup or substituting sunlight.

Stopping breastfeeding is rarely necessary

Most babies with jaundice can continue breastfeeding while receiving support, supplements if needed and phototherapy when indicated. Routine interruption can complicate feeding and reduce milk production without addressing the actual reason for the bilirubin rise.

In rare, selected circumstances a clinician may recommend a brief interruption, sometimes 12 to 48 hours, with repeat bilirubin testing. That is a supervised plan, not something to try at home to diagnose breast-milk jaundice. Agree on what the baby will receive, how milk will be expressed to maintain supply, when results will be checked and how breastfeeding will resume.

Persistent jaundice needs a clear follow-up plan

NICE advises assessment of jaundice lasting more than 14 days in babies born at 37 weeks or later, or more than 21 days in babies born earlier. These are review points, not promises that every normal baby must lose all yellow colouring by those dates. Other protocols may schedule tests differently according to feeding and clinical findings.

The team may measure direct or conjugated bilirubin, check the stool and urine history, review newborn screening and arrange other tests. Pale stools or dark urine should be reported immediately rather than waiting for the prolonged-jaundice deadline. Liver and bile-duct conditions need timely recognition.

Before leaving the birth unit or a jaundice appointment, write down the next contact and test date, the feeding plan and the symptoms that should bring you back sooner. If you feel that feeding or alertness is worsening, request reassessment even if a previous result was reassuring.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Bilirubin treatment thresholds depend on age in hours, gestational age and clinical risk; a single universal cutoff is unsafe.

Current feeding guidance supports continued breastfeeding in most cases, with individual supplementation or rare supervised interruption when indicated.

How BeMama can help

Keep the last bilirubin result, next test appointment, feeding plan and urgent contact number together so every caregiver can follow the same plan.

When to seek help

Jaundice in the first 24 hours, poor feeding, worsening sleepiness, pale stools or dark urine needs urgent assessment. Seizures, unresponsiveness, breathing problems or marked stiffness require emergency care.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Common newborn jaundice still needs appropriate assessment.
  • Low milk intake and breast-milk jaundice are different situations.
  • Visual colour cannot tell you the bilirubin level.
  • Home phototherapy requires clinical selection, prescribed equipment and monitoring.
  • Most babies can continue breastfeeding while jaundice is treated.

Frequently asked questions

Is jaundice normal in the first day after birth?

Jaundice within the first 24 hours needs urgent assessment. It should not be dismissed as ordinary newborn yellowing.

Can I judge the bilirubin level by how yellow the skin looks?

No. Appearance is unreliable, especially across different skin tones. A skin-meter reading or blood test and the baby’s age and risks guide care.

Is breastfeeding itself causing harm?

Usually not. Early jaundice may be related to insufficient intake, which needs feeding assessment. Later breast-milk jaundice is a different pattern and should be diagnosed after considering other causes.

What bilirubin number means my baby needs treatment?

There is no single number for every baby. The team uses age in hours, gestational age, the result and its trend, units and risk factors on an appropriate threshold chart.

Can I rent a lamp and treat jaundice at home?

Only within a supervised home-phototherapy plan after the baby is assessed as suitable. Correct equipment, daily or otherwise prescribed testing, feeding review and access to hospital care are essential.

Should I stop breastfeeding for two days?

Not routinely. Most babies continue breastfeeding. Any rare interruption should have a clinician-directed feeding, expression, retesting and restart plan.

Will extra water, sugar water or sunlight help?

These are not substitutes for effective milk feeding or prescribed phototherapy. Follow the newborn team’s plan rather than trying home remedies.

Why might extra milk be recommended?

It may be needed if intake is inadequate or the clinical situation requires it. Expressed milk, donor milk or formula may be considered alongside help to maintain breastfeeding.

When should persistent yellowing be checked?

Follow the local plan. NICE uses more than 14 days for babies born at or after 37 weeks and more than 21 days for earlier births. Pale stools or dark urine need attention immediately.

What if the last bilirubin result was reassuring but my baby is now difficult to wake?

Seek urgent medical help. A previous result does not override a new change in alertness, feeding or breathing; an unresponsive baby needs emergency care.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
